notes:
1. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — Overview

  • Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a jurist, economist, social reformer, political leader and constitutional thinker.
  • He became the foremost national leader in the struggle against caste discrimination and untouchability.
  • He served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
  • He became independent India's first Law Minister.
📌 Must-Memorise

B.R. Ambedkar → Social Justice + Constitution + Drafting Committee

2. Full Name

  • His full name was Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.
📌 Must-Memorise

B.R. → Bhimrao Ramji

3. Birth

  • Ambedkar was born on 14 April 1891.
  • His birthplace was Mhow in the Central Provinces of British India.
  • Mhow is now in Madhya Pradesh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → 14 April 1891 → Mhow

4. Present Name of Mhow

  • Mhow is now officially known as Dr. Ambedkar Nagar.

5. Father

  • Ambedkar's father was Ramji Maloji Sakpal.
  • He served in the British Indian Army.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar's Father → Ramji Maloji Sakpal

6. Mother

  • His mother was Bhimabai.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar's Mother → Bhimabai

7. Social Background

  • Ambedkar was born into the Mahar community.
  • The community was subjected to severe untouchability and caste discrimination under the prevailing social order.

8. Childhood Experience

  • Ambedkar personally experienced:
  • Segregation.
  • Denial of equal access.
  • Caste humiliation.
  • These experiences deeply influenced his later social and political work.

9. School Education

  • Ambedkar studied in Maharashtra.
  • He later attended Elphinstone High School in Bombay.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Elphinstone High School

10. Matriculation

  • He passed the matriculation examination in 1907.
  • His educational achievement was highly significant because access to higher education was severely restricted for oppressed communities.

11. Elphinstone College

  • Ambedkar continued his higher studies at Elphinstone College in Bombay.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Elphinstone College

12. Bombay University

  • He received his B.A. degree from the University of Bombay in 1912.

13. Subjects

His early university studies included:

  • Economics.
  • Political science.

Economics later became one of his principal academic specialisations.

14. Sayajirao Gaekwad III

  • Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda provided Ambedkar financial assistance for higher education abroad.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar's Overseas Scholarship → Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda

15. Columbia University

  • Ambedkar went to the United States in 1913.
  • He studied at Columbia University in New York.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Columbia University → 1913

16. Columbia and Intellectual Development

At Columbia he studied subjects including:

  • Economics.
  • Sociology.
  • History.
  • Political science.
  • Philosophy.

17. John Dewey

  • American philosopher John Dewey was one of Ambedkar's important intellectual influences at Columbia.
  • Dewey's ideas on:
  • Democracy.
  • Education.
  • Pragmatism.

influenced Ambedkar's thinking.

📌 Must-Memorise

John Dewey → Intellectual Influence on Ambedkar

18. M.A. Degree

  • Ambedkar obtained an M.A. from Columbia University in 1915.

19. Ancient Indian Commerce

  • One of Ambedkar's early academic works was Ancient Indian Commerce.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ancient Indian Commerce → Ambedkar

20. Castes in India

  • Ambedkar presented the paper Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development at Columbia University in 1916.
📌 Must-Memorise

Castes in India → Ambedkar → 1916

21. Importance of Castes in India

  • The work represented an early scholarly attempt by Ambedkar to analyse caste as a social institution.

22. Columbia Doctoral Research

  • Ambedkar conducted advanced research on public finance and the economic administration of British India.
  • His work later appeared as The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Evolution of Provincial Finance → Ambedkar

23. London

  • Ambedkar later moved to London for further studies.

24. London School of Economics

  • He studied economics at the London School of Economics.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → LSE

25. Gray's Inn

  • Ambedkar also joined Gray's Inn to study law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Gray's Inn → Law

26. Financial Difficulties

  • His overseas education was interrupted because of financial and scholarship constraints.
  • He later returned to London to complete his studies.

27. The Problem of the Rupee

  • Ambedkar's major economic work was The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution.
📌 Must-Memorise

The Problem of the Rupee → B.R. Ambedkar

28. Publication

  • The Problem of the Rupee was published in 1923.
  • It was based on Ambedkar's advanced research in monetary economics.

29. Main Subject of the Book

The work examined:

  • Indian currency.
  • Monetary policy.
  • Exchange rates.
  • Colonial financial arrangements.

30. Economics and Ambedkar

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ambedkar was not only a lawyer and constitutionalist.

He was also a formally trained:

  • Economist.
  • Public-finance scholar.

31. Bar-at-Law

  • Ambedkar completed his legal training in Britain and was called to the Bar through Gray's Inn.

32. Return to India

  • After his overseas education, Ambedkar built a career combining:
  • Law.
  • Teaching.
  • Journalism.
  • Social activism.
  • Politics.

33. Baroda Service

  • Under the terms of his earlier scholarship, Ambedkar briefly entered the service of the Baroda State.
  • He encountered severe caste discrimination despite his high educational qualifications.

34. Significance of Baroda Experience

  • His experience demonstrated that education alone did not automatically remove caste discrimination.

35. Bombay

  • Bombay became the principal centre of Ambedkar's professional, social and political activity.

36. Sydenham College

  • Ambedkar taught political economy at Sydenham College of Commerce and Economics in Bombay.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ambedkar → Professor of Political Economy

37. Legal Practice

  • Ambedkar later established himself as a lawyer in Bombay.
  • Legal training became important to his struggles for civil and constitutional rights.

38. Journalism

Ambedkar used newspapers and journals to:

  • Educate oppressed communities.
  • Criticise caste.
  • Demand political rights.
  • Build social organisation.

39. Mooknayak

  • Ambedkar launched the Marathi newspaper Mooknayak in 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mooknayak → Ambedkar → 1920

40. Meaning of Mooknayak

  • Mooknayak means "Leader of the Voiceless."
📌 Must-Memorise

Mooknayak → Leader of the Voiceless

41. Bahishkrit Bharat

  • Ambedkar later started the publication Bahishkrit Bharat in 1927.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahishkrit Bharat → Ambedkar

42. Janata

  • Janata was another important publication associated with Ambedkar's movement.

43. Prabuddha Bharat

  • Janata was later renamed Prabuddha Bharat.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ambedkar's Press → Mooknayak → Bahishkrit Bharat → Janata → Prabuddha Bharat

44. Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha

  • Ambedkar founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in 1924.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha → 1924 → Ambedkar

45. Purpose of the Sabha

It worked for:

  • Education.
  • Social uplift.
  • Economic advancement.
  • Political awareness of oppressed communities.

46. Ambedkar's Famous Call

Ambedkar's movement strongly emphasised:

  • Educate.
  • Agitate.
  • Organise.
📌 Must-Memorise

Educate, Agitate, Organise → Ambedkar

47. Education as Liberation

  • Ambedkar considered education essential for the emancipation of socially oppressed people.

48. Political Representation

He argued that oppressed communities needed:

  • Independent political organisation.
  • Representation.
  • Legal safeguards.
  • Access to education and employment.

49. Mahad Satyagraha

  • Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha in 1927.
  • It became one of the landmark anti-caste movements in modern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahad Satyagraha → 1927 → Ambedkar

50. Location of Mahad

  • Mahad is in present-day Maharashtra.

51. Chavdar Tank

  • The immediate issue was the right of the Depressed Classes to draw water from the public Chavdar Tank.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahad → Chavdar Tank → Public Water Rights

52. Civil Rights Character

  • Mahad was not merely a demand for water.
  • It asserted equal civic access to public resources.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mahad → Civil Equality

53. March 1927

  • The first major Mahad action took place in March 1927.

54. Opposition

  • Upper-caste opponents resisted the attempt to exercise equal access to the tank.
  • The struggle revealed the depth of caste exclusion.

55. Manusmriti Burning

  • On 25 December 1927, Ambedkar and his supporters publicly burned the Manusmriti at Mahad as a protest against caste hierarchy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Manusmriti Burning → Mahad → 25 December 1927

56. Significance of Manusmriti Burning

  • It symbolised rejection of religiously justified social inequality.

57. Samata Sainik Dal

  • Ambedkar's movement developed organisations to maintain discipline and mobilise supporters.
  • Samata Sainik Dal became an important volunteer organisation associated with his social movement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Samata Sainik Dal → Ambedkarite Movement

58. Temple Entry Question

  • Ambedkar also challenged restrictions preventing oppressed communities from entering Hindu temples.

59. Kalaram Temple Satyagraha

  • Ambedkar launched the Kalaram Temple entry movement at Nashik in 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kalaram Temple Satyagraha → Nashik → 1930

60. Kalaram Temple

  • Kalaram is a major Rama temple in Nashik.
  • Dalits were denied entry under prevailing caste practices.

61. Purpose of Temple Entry Campaign

The movement demanded:

  • Equal religious access.
  • Recognition of human dignity.
  • End of caste exclusion.

62. Ambedkar's Evolving Position

  • Over time Ambedkar became increasingly sceptical that caste equality could be achieved merely through reform within orthodox Hindu social structures.

63. Simon Commission

  • Ambedkar submitted evidence and views on political representation during the constitutional debates surrounding the Simon Commission.

64. Constitutional Politics

Ambedkar increasingly focused on securing:

  • Representation.
  • Electoral rights.
  • Political safeguards.
  • Civil equality.

65. Round Table Conferences

  • Three Round Table Conferences were held in London between 1930 and 1932.
  • Ambedkar participated in all three.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → All Three Round Table Conferences

66. First Round Table Conference

  • The First Round Table Conference began in 1930.
  • Congress did not officially participate.
  • Ambedkar represented the interests of the Depressed Classes.

67. Rettamalai Srinivasan

  • Tamil leader Rettamalai Srinivasan also represented the Depressed Classes at the Round Table Conference.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Ambedkar + Rettamalai Srinivasan → Depressed Classes Representation at Round Table Conference

68. Ambedkar's Demand

  • Ambedkar argued that political democracy would be incomplete without safeguards for socially oppressed communities.

69. Separate Electorates

  • Ambedkar initially supported separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
  • He believed independent political representation was necessary to prevent domination by socially powerful groups.

70. Second Round Table Conference

  • Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in 1931 as the principal representative of the Indian National Congress.
  • Ambedkar also participated.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi + Ambedkar → Second Round Table Conference → 1931

71. Gandhi–Ambedkar Difference

The principal dispute concerned:

  • Political representation of the Depressed Classes.
  • Separate electorates.

72. Communal Award

  • British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in August 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Communal Award → Ramsay MacDonald → 1932

73. Depressed Classes Under Communal Award

  • The Award provided separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

74. Gandhi's Opposition

  • Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
  • He feared that they would permanently divide Hindu society.

75. Yerwada Jail

  • Gandhi began a fast while imprisoned in Yerwada Central Jail at Pune in September 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact Context → Gandhi's Fast → Yerwada Jail

76. Negotiations

  • Intense negotiations followed between Ambedkar and Hindu political leaders.
  • A compromise was eventually reached.

77. Poona Pact

  • The Poona Pact was concluded on 24 September 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact → 24 September 1932

78. Poona Pact — Main Change

The Pact replaced:

Separate Electorates

with:

  • Joint electorates.
  • Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact → Joint Electorates + Reserved Seats

79. Provincial Reserved Seats

  • The Poona Pact substantially increased the number of reserved provincial legislative seats for the Depressed Classes to 148.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact → 148 Provincial Reserved Seats

80. Primary Elections

  • The Pact provided a system of preliminary elections among Depressed Class voters to help select candidates for reserved seats.

81. Gandhi and Ambedkar — Caution

  • The Poona Pact emerged from negotiations involving Ambedkar and representatives of caste Hindu political leadership while Gandhi was fasting.
  • It should not be reduced to a simple personal agreement between only two individuals.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Poona Pact → Wider Negotiated Settlement

82. Long-Term Significance of Poona Pact

  • Reserved representation later became an important part of India's constitutional framework for Scheduled Castes.

83. Yeola Conference

  • At the Yeola Conference in 1935, Ambedkar publicly declared his intention to leave Hinduism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Yeola Declaration → 1935

84. Famous Yeola Statement

Ambedkar declared in substance:

  • He had been born a Hindu but would not die a Hindu.
📌 Must-Memorise

"I will not die a Hindu" → Ambedkar → Yeola 1935

85. Annihilation of Caste

  • Ambedkar wrote Annihilation of Caste in 1936.
📌 Must-Memorise

Annihilation of Caste → 1936 → Ambedkar

86. Background of Annihilation of Caste

  • It was originally prepared as a speech for a caste-reform organisation.
  • The organisers objected to parts of the text.
  • Ambedkar published it independently.

87. Central Argument

  • Ambedkar argued that caste hierarchy could not be removed without challenging its ideological and religious foundations.

88. Importance

Annihilation of Caste became one of India's most influential texts on:

  • Caste.
  • Equality.
  • Social democracy.

89. Independent Labour Party

  • Ambedkar founded the Independent Labour Party in 1936.
📌 Must-Memorise

Independent Labour Party → 1936 → Ambedkar

90. Social Base

The Independent Labour Party addressed issues affecting:

  • Industrial workers.
  • Agricultural labourers.
  • Oppressed castes.

91. Bombay Elections

  • The party contested the 1937 provincial elections in the Bombay Presidency and won representation in the legislature.

92. Labour and Caste

  • Ambedkar argued that economic exploitation and caste oppression had to be addressed together.

93. Khoti System

  • Ambedkar opposed exploitative land-tenure arrangements such as the Khoti system in parts of the Bombay Presidency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ambedkar → Labour + Agrarian Reform, Not Only Caste Issues

94. Mahar Watan

  • Ambedkar also challenged hereditary service arrangements that burdened Mahar communities.

95. Labour Rights

Ambedkar advocated:

  • Better working conditions.
  • Social security.
  • Labour welfare.
  • Economic justice.

96. Scheduled Castes Federation

  • Ambedkar founded the All India Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942.
📌 Must-Memorise

Scheduled Castes Federation → 1942 → Ambedkar

97. Purpose of Scheduled Castes Federation

It aimed to provide an independent political platform for:

  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Social justice demands.
  • Political representation.

98. Viceroy's Executive Council

  • Ambedkar served on the Viceroy's Executive Council from 1942 to 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Viceroy's Executive Council → 1942–46

99. Labour Member

  • He served as Labour Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Labour Member

100. Labour Policy

During this period, Ambedkar dealt with matters relating to:

  • Labour welfare.
  • Employment.
  • Industrial relations.
  • Water and power policy.

101. Eight-Hour Workday

  • Ambedkar is strongly associated with labour-policy efforts supporting regulation of working hours and improved industrial welfare.
  • The broader history of the eight-hour workday involved legislation and policy development over several years.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Do Not Reduce the Entire Eight-Hour Workday History to a Single Individual or Date

102. Water Resources

  • Ambedkar showed strong interest in:
  • Irrigation.
  • Multipurpose river projects.
  • Power development.
  • Economic planning.

103. Economic Planning

  • Ambedkar argued for industrialisation and state-led economic development as tools of social transformation.

104. States and Minorities

  • Ambedkar wrote States and Minorities in 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

States and Minorities → Ambedkar → 1947

105. States and Minorities — Themes

It dealt with:

  • Fundamental rights.
  • Minority safeguards.
  • Economic democracy.
  • State responsibility.

106. Thoughts on Pakistan

  • Ambedkar analysed the political question of Pakistan in a major work first published as Thoughts on Pakistan.

107. Pakistan or the Partition of India

  • The work later appeared in expanded form as Pakistan or the Partition of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pakistan or the Partition of India → Ambedkar

108. Who Were the Shudras?

  • Ambedkar published Who Were the Shudras? in 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Who Were the Shudras? → 1946

109. The Untouchables

  • Ambedkar wrote The Untouchables: Who Were They and Why They Became Untouchables?
📌 Must-Memorise

The Untouchables → Ambedkar

110. Waiting for a Visa

  • Waiting for a Visa is an autobiographical account associated with Ambedkar.
  • It describes personal experiences of caste discrimination.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Waiting for a Visa → Ambedkar's Experiences of Untouchability

111. Constituent Assembly

  • Ambedkar became a member of the Constituent Assembly.
  • He initially entered from Bengal.

112. Bengal Seat

  • His original Constituent Assembly seat was affected by the Partition of India.

113. Bombay Presidency Seat

  • Ambedkar subsequently entered the Constituent Assembly from the Bombay Presidency.

114. Drafting Committee

  • The Constituent Assembly appointed the Drafting Committee on 29 August 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

Drafting Committee → 29 August 1947

115. Chairman of Drafting Committee

  • B.R. Ambedkar was appointed Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chairman, Drafting Committee → B.R. Ambedkar

116. Other Drafting Committee Members

The original committee included:

  • B.R. Ambedkar.
  • N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar.
  • Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar.
  • K.M. Munshi.
  • Mohammad Saadulla.
  • B.L. Mitter.
  • D.P. Khaitan.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Drafting Committee Membership → Frequent Matching Question

117. Changes in Membership

  • B.L. Mitter resigned because of ill health.
  • N. Madhava Rau later replaced him.
  • D.P. Khaitan died and was replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

T.T. Krishnamachari → Drafting Committee Replacement Member

118. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar

  • Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar was a distinguished jurist from the Madras Presidency and an original member of the Drafting Committee.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar → Drafting Committee

119. Constitutional Adviser

  • B.N. Rau served as Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly.
  • He was not a member of the Drafting Committee.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

B.N. Rau → Constitutional Adviser

Ambedkar → Drafting Committee Chairman

120. Ambedkar's Constitutional Role

Ambedkar played a major role in explaining and defending:

  • Draft Constitution.
  • Fundamental rights.
  • Federal arrangements.
  • Parliamentary government.
  • Constitutional remedies.

121. Constitutional Morality

  • Ambedkar emphasised the importance of constitutional morality for a successful democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitutional Morality → Strongly Associated with Ambedkar's Constitutional Thought

122. Political Democracy

For Ambedkar, political democracy required more than elections.

It required:

  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Fraternity.

123. Social Democracy

  • Ambedkar argued that political democracy could not survive without social democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Social Democracy = Liberty + Equality + Fraternity

124. Liberty, Equality and Fraternity

  • Ambedkar treated liberty, equality and fraternity as mutually dependent principles.

125. Fraternity

  • Fraternity was especially important in his vision of building social unity in a caste-divided society.

126. Article 32

  • Ambedkar regarded Article 32 as one of the most important provisions of the Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 32 → Constitutional Remedies

127. "Heart and Soul"

  • Ambedkar famously described the constitutional-remedies provision as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Heart and Soul of Constitution → Article 32

128. Article 17

  • Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 17 → Abolition of Untouchability

129. Equality

Ambedkar strongly supported constitutional guarantees relating to:

  • Equality before law.
  • Non-discrimination.
  • Equal opportunity.

130. Reservations

  • Constitutional safeguards were designed to improve representation of historically disadvantaged communities.
  • Reservation developed as one instrument of protective discrimination/social justice.

131. Parliamentary Democracy

  • Ambedkar supported parliamentary government while repeatedly warning that institutions depended on democratic behaviour and constitutional morality.

132. Federalism

  • The Constitution established a federal structure with a comparatively strong Union government.
  • Ambedkar defended a strong Centre in the context of India's political circumstances.

133. Fundamental Rights

  • Ambedkar regarded enforceable rights as essential protections against arbitrary power and social discrimination.

134. Directive Principles

  • The Constitution also included Directive Principles directed toward social and economic democracy.

135. Constitution Adopted

  • The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitution Adopted → 26 November 1949

136. Constitution Came into Force

  • The Constitution came fully into force on 26 January 1950.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitution in Force → 26 January 1950

137. Draft Constitution Introduction

  • Ambedkar introduced the Draft Constitution for discussion in the Constituent Assembly in November 1948.

138. Constitutional Warnings

In his final Constituent Assembly speeches, Ambedkar warned against:

  • Hero worship in politics.
  • Unconstitutional methods.
  • Social and economic inequality.

139. Constitutional Methods

  • Ambedkar argued that after constitutional democratic methods became available, political change should ordinarily be pursued through constitutional processes.

140. Hero Worship

  • He warned that excessive devotion to political leaders could threaten democracy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ambedkar → Warning Against Hero Worship in Politics

141. Contradiction in Indian Democracy

  • Ambedkar warned that India was entering political equality while continuing to face severe social and economic inequality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Political Equality vs Social-Economic Inequality → Ambedkar's Warning

142. First Law Minister

  • Ambedkar became the first Law Minister of independent India.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Law Minister of India → B.R. Ambedkar

143. Nehru Cabinet

  • Ambedkar served in Jawaharlal Nehru's first Cabinet.

144. Hindu Code Bill

  • As Law Minister, Ambedkar strongly supported comprehensive reform of Hindu personal law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hindu Code Bill → Ambedkar

145. Objectives of Hindu Code Reform

The proposals addressed matters such as:

  • Marriage.
  • Divorce.
  • Inheritance.
  • Property rights.
  • Women's legal position.

146. Opposition

  • The Hindu Code Bill faced significant political and social opposition.

147. Resignation

  • Ambedkar resigned from the Union Cabinet in 1951.
  • The failure to secure progress on the Hindu Code Bill was a major reason for his resignation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar Resigned as Law Minister → 1951

148. Women's Rights

  • Ambedkar regarded improvement of women's legal rights as essential to social democracy.

149. Ambedkar on Women

His work addressed:

  • Property rights.
  • Marriage reform.
  • Labour protection.
  • Political equality.

150. Election Politics

  • Ambedkar contested elections after independence but did not always achieve electoral success.
  • His influence remained much broader than his electoral representation.

151. Rajya Sabha

  • Ambedkar later served as a member of the Rajya Sabha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Rajya Sabha in Final Years

152. Republican Party Idea

  • Ambedkar envisioned a broader political organisation known as the Republican Party.
  • The Republican Party of India was formally established after his death.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Republican Party of India → Formed After Ambedkar's Death

153. Religion and Ambedkar

  • Ambedkar spent many years studying:
  • Buddhism.
  • Hinduism.
  • Sikhism.
  • Christianity.
  • Islam.
  • He considered religion important only when compatible with morality and social equality.

154. Decision to Convert

  • His 1935 Yeola declaration began a long period of consideration about religious conversion.

155. Choice of Buddhism

  • Ambedkar ultimately chose Buddhism.
  • He interpreted Buddhism as a religion of:
  • Equality.
  • Reason.
  • Morality.
  • Compassion.

156. Buddhist Conversion

  • Ambedkar formally converted to Buddhism on 14 October 1956.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar's Conversion → 14 October 1956

157. Deekshabhoomi

  • The conversion ceremony took place at Nagpur.
  • The site is known as Deekshabhoomi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deekshabhoomi → Nagpur → Ambedkar

158. Bhante Chandramani

  • Buddhist monk Bhante Chandramani administered the initial Buddhist vows to Ambedkar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhante Chandramani → Ambedkar's Buddhist Conversion

159. Mass Conversion

  • Hundreds of thousands of followers joined the Buddhist conversion movement at Nagpur.

160. Twenty-Two Vows

  • Ambedkar administered a set of 22 vows to his followers during the conversion ceremony.
📌 Must-Memorise

22 Vows → Ambedkar's Buddhist Conversion

161. Navayana

  • The modern Buddhist movement inspired by Ambedkar is often described as Navayana, or "New Vehicle."
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Navayana Buddhism → B.R. Ambedkar

162. The Buddha and His Dhamma

  • Ambedkar's major Buddhist work was The Buddha and His Dhamma.
📌 Must-Memorise

The Buddha and His Dhamma → Ambedkar

163. Publication

  • The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously in 1957.
📌 Must-Memorise

The Buddha and His Dhamma → Published 1957

164. Buddhism and Social Ethics

Ambedkar emphasised Buddhist principles such as:

  • Prajna.
  • Karuna.
  • Samata.

Broadly:

  • Wisdom.
  • Compassion.
  • Equality.

165. Death

  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956 in Delhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Died 6 December 1956

166. Mahaparinirvan Diwas

  • 6 December is commemorated by followers as Mahaparinirvan Diwas.

167. Chaitya Bhoomi

  • Ambedkar was cremated at Dadar in Bombay.
  • The memorial site is known as Chaitya Bhoomi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chaitya Bhoomi → Mumbai → Ambedkar

168. Deekshabhoomi vs Chaitya Bhoomi

  • Deekshabhoomi → Nagpur → Conversion.

174. Economic Works

Important economic writings include:

  • Ancient Indian Commerce.
  • The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India.
  • The Problem of the Rupee.

175. Social Works

Important works include:

  • Castes in India.
  • Annihilation of Caste.
  • Who Were the Shudras?
  • The Untouchables.

176. Political-Constitutional Works

Important writings include:

  • States and Minorities.
  • Pakistan or the Partition of India.
  • Constitutional speeches and interventions.

177. Ambedkar and Democracy

For Ambedkar, democracy was:

  • Not simply a form of government.
  • Also a mode of social association based on equality and respect.

178. Social Justice

Ambedkar's social-justice programme centred on:

  • Dignity.
  • Equality.
  • Education.
  • Representation.
  • Economic opportunity.

179. Caste and Democracy

  • Ambedkar regarded caste as fundamentally incompatible with genuine fraternity and social democracy.

180. Caste and Division of Labour

  • Ambedkar criticised the claim that caste was merely a division of labour.
  • He argued that it was a hierarchical division of labourers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ambedkar → Critique of Caste as Hierarchical Social Division

181. Equality Before Law

  • He insisted that formal legal equality must be supported by social and economic transformation.

182. Reservations and Representation

Ambedkar's political strategy recognised that historically excluded groups required mechanisms to secure effective participation in:

  • Legislatures.
  • Public employment.
  • Education.

183. Ambedkar and Labour

His public career included major engagement with:

  • Factory workers.
  • Working hours.
  • Wages.
  • Industrial disputes.
  • Labour welfare.

184. Ambedkar and Agriculture

  • Ambedkar also examined problems of:
  • Small landholdings.
  • Agrarian productivity.
  • Rural poverty.

185. Industrialisation

  • He favoured industrialisation partly because excessive dependence on agriculture trapped large populations in low-productivity employment.

186. Ambedkar and Monetary Policy

  • The Problem of the Rupee remains important evidence of Ambedkar's expertise in monetary economics.

187. Reserve Bank Connection — Caution

  • Ambedkar's monetary analysis contributed to contemporary debates on Indian currency and central banking.
  • However, it is inaccurate to say that Ambedkar alone "founded" the Reserve Bank of India.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

RBI Founded 1935 → Do Not Attribute Its Creation Solely to Ambedkar

188. Ambedkar and Education

He treated education as:

  • A means of self-respect.
  • A route to economic advancement.
  • A weapon against social oppression.

189. People's Education Society

  • Ambedkar founded the People's Education Society in 1945.
📌 Must-Memorise

People's Education Society → 1945 → Ambedkar

190. Siddharth College

  • The People's Education Society established Siddharth College in Bombay.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Siddharth College → Ambedkar's Educational Movement

191. Milind College

  • Ambedkar's educational movement was also associated with Milind College at Aurangabad.

192. Political Independence vs Social Freedom

  • Ambedkar repeatedly argued that freedom from British rule would be incomplete without freedom from internal social oppression.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → Political Freedom + Social Freedom

193. Ambedkar and National Movement

  • Ambedkar frequently disagreed with Congress and Gandhi on methods and representation.
  • Yet his constitutional and social struggles formed an essential part of modern India's democratic transformation.

194. Gandhi and Ambedkar

They agreed on the need to end untouchability but differed sharply on:

  • Caste.
  • Political representation.
  • Separate electorates.
  • Social reform strategy.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Gandhi and Ambedkar → Both Opposed Untouchability, But Their Approaches Differed

195. Harijan Term — Ambedkar's Position

  • Gandhi used the term Harijan for communities subjected to untouchability.
  • Ambedkar did not adopt Gandhi's terminology as the basis of his political movement.

196. Depressed Classes

  • "Depressed Classes" was a common colonial-era administrative and political term.
  • The Constitution later used the category Scheduled Castes.

197. Scheduled Castes

  • Constitutional provisions created safeguards for Scheduled Castes in independent India.

198. Tamil Nadu Link — Rettamalai Srinivasan

  • Rettamalai Srinivasan and Ambedkar were both prominent representatives of oppressed communities in national constitutional debates.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Rettamalai Srinivasan ↔ Ambedkar → Representation of Depressed Classes

199. Tamil Nadu Link — M.C. Rajah

  • M.C. Rajah of the Madras Presidency was another important early leader of the Depressed Classes.
  • He participated in debates on political representation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

M.C. Rajah → Depressed Classes Politics → Madras Presidency

200. Rajah–Moonje Pact

  • M.C. Rajah and B.S. Moonje reached an agreement in 1932 favouring reserved seats within joint electorates.
  • It formed part of the wider debate preceding the Poona Pact.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

M.C. Rajah → Representation Debate Before Poona Pact

201. Tamil Nadu and Ambedkarite Thought

  • Ambedkar's writings later exercised strong influence on anti-caste and social-justice politics in Tamil Nadu.

202. Ambedkar and Periyar

  • Ambedkar and Periyar shared strong opposition to caste hierarchy.
  • Their political strategies and intellectual frameworks were not identical.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Ambedkar ≠ Periyar

Shared Anti-Caste Objective, Different Political Traditions
